plan: Leaning on types raters found hard: uncommon vocabulary (phlegmatic), inverted compound-subject agreement, a confound completion, and a counterexample data item; S011-08 resubmitted with a sharpened goal.

passages.title: Unmoved characters
passages.text: Critics found the director's latest film strangely ______: although its plot is crowded with explosions and chases, its characters display almost no emotion, greeting each new disaster with the same mild interest.

passages.title: Reproduced results
passages.text: The chemist's early claims about the new catalyst were initially met with skepticism, but they were ______ by later experiments, which reproduced her results in three independent laboratories.

passages.title: Hidden letters
passages.text: Beneath the floorboards of the old farmhouse ______ a bundle of letters and two photographs that had been hidden there for nearly a century.

passages.title: Two researchers
passages.text: The two ______ findings, published a month apart, seemed to contradict each other until a third team showed that the studies had measured soil moisture at different depths.

passages.title: Trees and asthma
passages.text: A city found that children in neighborhoods with many street trees had lower rates of asthma than children in neighborhoods with few trees. A council member concluded that planting more trees would reduce childhood asthma. The tree-lined neighborhoods, however, also had ______

passages.title: Light and growth
passages.text:
A botanist grew three plant species under red, blue, and white light and recorded average height, in centimeters, after six weeks.
Species | Red | Blue | White
X | 20 | 18 | 15
Y | 14 | 17 | 12
Z | 25 | 21 | 19
A student claims that red light produced the tallest plants for every species in the study.

passages.title: Seventy-year dictionary
passages.text: The first edition of one major English dictionary took about seventy years to complete, from the collection of the first quotations to the publication of the final volume. ______ by the time the last volume appeared, the earliest volumes were already out of date, missing words that had entered the language in the meantime.

passages.title: Museum notes
passages.text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• The Harlan Museum displays each object with only a short label giving its name and date.
• Curators there want visitors to form their own impressions before reading about an object.
• The Ostrova Museum places a long text panel and an audio guide beside each object.
• Curators there want visitors to understand each object's history in detail.

passages.title: Solar storm
passages.text: In 1859, a powerful solar storm produced auroras visible as far south as the Caribbean. Telegraph operators reported sparks leaping from their equipment, and some found they could send messages even after disconnecting their batteries. Scientists today estimate that a storm of similar strength would seriously damage modern power grids and satellites.

passages.title: Crow study notes
passages.text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Researchers wore a distinctive mask while trapping and banding several wild crows.
• The crows were then released unharmed.
• In later years, crows on the campus scolded and dived at people wearing that mask.
• The crows largely ignored people wearing a different mask.
• Researchers concluded that crows can recognize and remember individual human faces.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
candidates.evidence: its characters display almost no emotion, greeting each new disaster with the same mild interest
candidates.explanation: The characters stay calm and unemotional amid chaos: "phlegmatic." "Although" sets their calm against the frantic plot.

A.rationale: "Frenetic" fits the explosions and chases, but the colon clause describes the characters' lack of emotion.

C.rationale: Melodramatic characters show exaggerated emotion, the opposite of what is described.

D.rationale: "Convoluted" describes a tangled plot, not the characters' calm.

hints: Does the blank describe the plot or the characters?
candidates.remember: Check which part of the sentence the blank describes.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
candidates.evidence: which reproduced her results in three independent laboratories
candidates.explanation: Independent reproduction confirms a claim: the claims were "borne out."

A.rationale: Later experiments cannot anticipate earlier claims.

B.rationale: Reproducing her results supports the claims; it does not undermine them.

D.rationale: The experiments confirmed the claims rather than drawing attention away from them.

hints: Did the later experiments support or weaken the claims?

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.evidence: a bundle of letters and two photographs
candidates.explanation: The sentence is inverted; the subject follows the verb and is compound (a bundle ... and two photographs), so it takes the plural "were."

A.rationale: "Was" agrees only with the nearby "bundle," but the subject is "a bundle ... and two photographs."

C.rationale: "Is" is singular and shifts out of the past tense.

hints: Where is the subject in this sentence?
Is the subject singular or compound?

strategy.explanation: Flip the sentence: "a bundle ... and two photographs ___ beneath ..."

candidates.remember: Compound subjects joined by "and" are plural, even after the verb.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.explanation: Two researchers each produced findings, so the plural possessive "researchers'" is correct.

A.rationale: "Researcher's" is singular, but two researchers produced the findings.

B.rationale: Without an apostrophe, the word does not show possession.

C.rationale: A plural ending in s takes only an apostrophe.

candidates.remember: Plural possessive: add an apostrophe after the s.

candidates.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: more parks and playgrounds, where children often spend time playing outdoors.
choices.B: fewer factories and less truck traffic, both major sources of air pollution.
choices.C: older houses, many of which had recently been painted and renovated.
choices.D: higher rates of asthma among adults than among the children studied.

candidates.evidence: A council member concluded that planting more trees would reduce childhood asthma.
candidates.explanation: "However" signals a reason to doubt the council member's conclusion. Less air pollution in the same neighborhoods is an alternative explanation for lower asthma.

A.rationale: More outdoor time does not obviously explain lower asthma rates; it is not a clear alternative cause.

C.rationale: Renovation is not linked to asthma in the text.

D.rationale: Adult rates do not explain the children's difference.

hints: What does "however" suggest the blank will do to the conclusion?

strategy.explanation: Predict an alternative cause of lower asthma.

candidates.remember: A confounding factor offers another explanation for a correlation.

candidates.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to weaken the student's claim?

choices.A: Species Z averaged 25 centimeters under red light, the tallest height recorded in the study.
choices.B: Species X averaged 15 centimeters under white light, shorter than under either red or blue.
choices.C: Species Y averaged 17 centimeters under blue light, taller than its 14 centimeters under red.
choices.D: Species Y averaged 12 centimeters under white light, the shortest height recorded for Y.

candidates.evidence: red light produced the tallest plants for every species
candidates.explanation: The claim says red produced the tallest plants for every species. Species Y grew taller under blue (17) than under red (14), a counterexample.

A.rationale: This is consistent with the claim.

B.rationale: This is consistent with the claim.

D.rationale: White being shortest does not contradict red being tallest.

hints: A claim about "every species" is weakened by one exception.
Which species did not grow tallest under red?

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
candidates.evidence: took about seventy years to complete
candidates.explanation: Because the project took seventy years, the early volumes aged before it finished: a consequence.

A.rationale: "Nevertheless" signals a contrast, but outdated volumes follow from the long timeline.

C.rationale: Outdated volumes are a result, not an example, of the long timeline.

hints: Why would the earliest volumes be out of date?
candidates.remember: Name the relationship before choosing the transition.

candidates.stem: The student wants to contrast how the two museums present information to visitors. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: The Harlan uses short labels so visitors judge first; the Ostrova adds long panels and audio.
choices.B: Curators at both the Harlan and the Ostrova want visitors to engage closely with each object in the collection.
choices.C: The Ostrova Museum places a long text panel and an audio guide beside each object in its collection.
choices.D: The Harlan Museum gives each object a short label, and its curators prefer that visitors form impressions first.

candidates.evidence: The Ostrova Museum places a long text panel and an audio guide beside each object.
candidates.explanation: A contrast requires both museums and their difference: minimal labels versus extensive panels and audio. Only A does both.

B.rationale: This states a similarity, not a contrast.

hints: Does each choice mention both museums?
candidates.remember: Contrast answers must name both things being contrasted.

candidates.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the second sentence in the overall structure of the text?

choices.A: It explains the scientific cause of the auroras that people saw during the storm.
choices.B: It presents evidence that the storm's strength has been greatly exaggerated.
choices.C: It shows the storm's effects on 1859 technology, setting up the modern comparison.
choices.D: It shows how telegraph operators learned to prevent damage from solar storms.

candidates.evidence: Telegraph operators reported sparks leaping from their equipment
candidates.explanation: Sentence 1 introduces the storm; sentence 2 gives its effects on 1859 technology (telegraphs); sentence 3 projects similar effects on modern technology.

A.rationale: The sentence describes effects on telegraphs, not the cause of auroras.

D.rationale: Sending messages without batteries was a strange effect, not a prevention method.

hints: How does sentence 2 connect to sentence 3?
candidates.remember: Middle sentences often bridge a setup and a conclusion.

candidates.stem: The student wants to describe the study and present its key finding to an audience unfamiliar with it. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: Crows scolded people in the mask worn by their trappers, suggesting crows remember individual humans.
choices.B: Researchers wearing a distinctive mask trapped several wild crows, banded them, and released them unharmed.
choices.C: In later years, crows on the campus scolded and dived at some people but largely ignored others.
choices.D: Crows can recognize and remember individual human faces, according to the researchers in the study.

candidates.evidence: Researchers concluded that crows can recognize and remember individual human faces.
candidates.explanation: The goal now has two parts, describing the study and presenting the finding. Only A does both: it describes the mask setup and the crows' response, then states what that suggests.

B.rationale: This describes the method, not the finding.

C.rationale: Without the masks, this does not explain what the crows recognized.

D.rationale: This states the conclusion but does not describe the study.

hints: What does an unfamiliar audience need to understand the finding?

strategy.explanation: Check for both the observation and the conclusion.

candidates.remember: A finding for a new audience needs evidence and meaning.
candidates.revision_note: S011-08 resubmitted: the goal now explicitly requires describing the study as well as the finding, so D (finding only) is clearly incomplete; A reworded to avoid overreaching from masks to faces.
